# Re-filling the Coolant - Suzuki Ritz (Splash) Diesel

Restoring the cooling system on a Suzuki Ritz or Splash with the DDIS diesel engine requires a methodical approach to ensure you aren't just toping up water, but actually flushing out the dilution that has occurred. When coolant levels have been maintained via frequent topping-ups for an extended period, the organic additives essential for corrosion inhibition and lubrication are often leached out of the system, leaving behind a mixture that is predominantly plain water. This state is dangerous because while water transfers heat effectively, it lacks the chemical properties to protect the aluminum components in your radiator and the iron/grey cast iron in your engine block from galvanic corrosion.

The first step involves locating the drain point. On this specific model, there is no cap on the main radiator neck; instead, the pressure release and fill mechanism is located on the plastic overflow reservoir situated near the battery. To fully drain the system, you will need to access the coolant drain bolt located at the very bottom of the engine block or the lower part of the radiator tank. This bolt is typically found behind the oil filter housing or directly underneath the passenger side of the engine bay. You will need a 10mm socket and a ratchet extension to reach it comfortably. Once accessible, loosen the drain plug carefully while the engine is cold. Allow the fluid to empty completely into a waste container. Do not attempt this operation with an overheating engine, as the system is under significant pressure; releasing that pressure instantly can result in scalding coolant spraying onto your skin or eyes.

Once the old fluid has drained, you must select the correct replacement medium. The Suzuki DDIS engine requires a specific type of antifreeze, usually specified by the manufacturer as a green or orange ethylene glycol-based coolant compatible with G12/G13 standards, though exact specifications can vary by market year. It is crucial to avoid mixing incompatible coolant types (e.g., mixing old green coolant with new orange OAT fluid) as this creates precipitates that clog narrow passages in the heater core and radiator. The standard operating procedure dictates a specific mixture ratio: generally, a 50/50 mix of coolant concentrate and distilled water is recommended for most climates. Using tap water is not advisable due to dissolved minerals that can form scale deposits on the heat exchanger surfaces, reducing thermal efficiency over time.

After refilling the system with fresh coolant through the reservoir cap, the final verification step is critical. Before starting the engine, ensure all hose clamps and the drain bolt are securely tightened. Start the engine and let it reach operating temperature while the heater is set to maximum. This allows the thermostat to open and circulates fluid through the entire loop, including the heater core. Watch the coolant level in the reservoir; it will drop as air bubbles escape from the system. Top up the mixture gradually until it stabilizes at the "MAX" mark on the cold side of the reservoir. Check for leaks around the drain plug and hose connections while the engine runs. If the fluid was significantly diluted, consider performing a pressure test after the initial fill to ensure there are no micro-leaks that might go unnoticed visually.
